5. Mr. S. S. Haider, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant-pre-emptor submitted that in the written objection there was no specific statement that Sayera Khatun was a co-sharer and, as such, the pre-emptor had no opportunity for adding her as a party. 

 6. Mr. Rafiqur Rahman, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents on the other hand has contended that the pre-emptor did not take any steps to meet the objection of the defect of parties raised in the written statement by serving any interrogatory upon the pre-emptee and that the law enjoins upon the pre-emptor to implead all the co-sharers as parties and, as such, the pre-emption has been rightly refused in this case. 

 7. 33 DLR (A.D) 113 has laid down the law regarding necessary parties in a pre-emption application under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. There it has been held :— 

 8. It will thus appear that Sayera Khatun being found to be a co-sharer she was a necessary party in the pre-emption proceeding and the failure to make her party to the pre-emption proceeding has vitiated the pre-emption case. The mere fact that the respondent did not disclose her name does not absolve the appellant-pre-emptors from his mandatory duty to implead her by ascertaining necessary particulars. Because the pre-emptors could not be oblivious as to Ext. B(2) the kabala dated 2.6.73 by which Sayera Khatun purchased 1.40 acres of land out of the disputed tenancy and ought to have made her a party. The contention of Mr. Haldar is untenable because not only the objection was taken in the written statement about non-joinder of necessary party, Ext. B(2) would have clarified as to who has been left out. The pre-emptor did not take any step and failed to remove the defect. 

 9. For the reasons stated above we hold that the pre-emption has been rightly refused. This appeal is, therefore, dismissed but there will be no order as to costs.
